analysis.one_liner: Bans federal judges from owning stocks, requires Supreme Court ethics rules, and limits secret settlements.
analysis.headline: The judicial ethics bill, backed by 44 House Democrats including sponsor Pramila Jayapal, was sent to six House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set binding ethics rules for federal judges and Supreme Court justices: no individual stocks or hedge funds, no corporate board seats, stricter gift limits, and public lists of conflicts requiring a judge to step aside. It would have applied the judges' Code of Conduct to the Supreme Court for the first time, created a committee to review complaints against justices, and barred courts from sealing case records or settlements that hide dangers to public health or safety. It was referred to six House committees, none of which acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary litigants and the general public. If the bill had passed, judges deciding cases could no longer hold stock in companies appearing before them; Supreme Court justices would be subject to a written ethics code with a complaint process; gifts from sponsors of private judicial seminars would be banned; and corporations could no longer bury evidence of product dangers or safety hazards behind sealed settlements and protective orders, which also protects consumers, workers, and neighbors of polluting facilities. Court records, speeches, and recusal decisions would be posted online in accessible formats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Court litigants and the general public

how_it_helps.text: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices could no longer own or trade individual stocks, hedge fund interests, derivatives, or stakes in closely held businesses; violators would face civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation enforceable by the Attorney General or Special Counsel.

The Code of Conduct for U.S. Judges would apply to Supreme Court justices, and a five-member Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee would receive and investigate complaints against justices, with findings referred to the House Judiciary Committee.

Each judge would have to file a public list of every association or financial interest requiring recusal, including a spouse's or minor child's interests, and litigants could petition for a judge's disqualification with a public written explanation required.

Gifts connected to private, sponsor-funded judicial seminars would be prohibited, and a taxpayer-funded Judicial Education Fund would cover seminar costs instead, so a few thousand dollars a year per program would no longer come from litigants' industries.

Courts could not enforce settlement agreements or protective orders that hide information relevant to public health or safety, and could not gag parties from reporting hazards to federal or state regulators, ending the practice of sealing evidence of dangerous products or contamination.

Audio of appellate and Supreme Court sessions would be posted online, judges' speeches made public, case-assignment data published, and retired judges could still face misconduct complaints, including pension reductions.

analysis.who_pays: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices who currently hold individual stocks, corporate board seats, or business interests would have to divest them (with a government-run Federal Employee Investment Account as an alternative). Corporate defendants and their law firms would lose the ability to seal litigation records and settlements that involve public health or safety risks. Sponsors of privately funded judicial seminars could no longer provide judges with free travel and lodging, and taxpayers would fund a roughly $3 million-per-year Judicial Education Fund and the new review committee.
analysis.who_pays_short: Judges with stock holdings and litigating corporations

drawbacks.text: The bill raises separation-of-powers questions: Congress would be imposing an ethics code, a complaints committee, and disclosure duties on the judicial branch, including the Supreme Court, and the constitutional questions would likely have drawn litigation if the bill had passed.

Mandatory divestment of all individual securities, with only diversified funds, Treasury bonds, and a new Federal Employee Investment Account allowed, is stricter than the rules that apply to members of Congress and could deter experienced lawyers and businesspeople from accepting judgeships.

Taxpayers would bear new costs: $3 million per year for the Judicial Education Fund plus the staffing and compensation of the new Supreme Court Complaints Review Committee, whose proceedings are largely confidential.

Restrictions on sealing settlements, while aimed at hidden public dangers, would make some corporate defendants more willing to fight cases to judgment rather than settle, which can mean longer, costlier litigation for the injured people those settlements pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — judges without personal financial stakes in their cases, a Supreme Court subject to a written ethics code, and safety hazards that can no longer be hidden behind sealed settlements — are substantial and hard to obtain any other way, since the judiciary does not police itself. The costs are real but modest: taxpayer funding for judicial education and a review committee, some constitutional friction with the judicial branch, and less confidentiality in settlements. On balance the design addresses a documented gap in oversight of the highest court, though the broad divestment mandate is more sweeping than comparable rules for members of Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to six House committees on the day it was introduced; none of them ever held a hearing or sent it anywhere, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Judicial Ethics and Anti-Corruption Act of 2023 on June 9, 2023, joined by 43 Democratic cosponsors.

The bill was referred the same day to six committees — Judiciary, Oversight and Accountability, Rules, Financial Services, Agriculture, and House Administration — a referral pattern that splits a bill across committees with competing claims on it.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup appears in the action history, and the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate during the 118th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died with it; all legislative work would have had to start over in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting federal judges and Supreme Court justices keep the current system of self-enforced ethics, stock ownership, and acceptance of privately funded seminar travel. Corporate defendants likewise keep the ability to seal records and settlements that would otherwise disclose health and safety hazards, because the provision that would have limited that never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Judges with stock portfolios and litigating corporations

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Judicial Ethics and Anti-Corruption Act of 2023 on June 9, 2023.

for.name: 43 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from the House Democratic caucus; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling committee agendas and floor scheduling in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to six committees on its introduction day and never scheduled any committee action or floor vote on it during the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill, the first step usually required to move a bill out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the House's 224 Republicans, who controlled the committees and the floor schedule, took no action on the bill, and the record shows no Republican support for it.

industries.industry: Federal judges and Supreme Court justices
industries.note: The bill would force divestment of individual stocks, ban corporate board seats, restrict gifts, and create external complaint and review processes covering the Supreme Court. Judges currently set their own ethics rules through the Judicial Conference, and the bill would have moved that power toward Congress and public enforcement.

industries.industry: Corporations facing health and safety litigation (drug, chemical, product, and energy companies)
industries.note: The bill would bar courts from enforcing settlements and protective orders that hide information about public health or safety hazards and would protect whistleblowers who report to regulators. These companies currently use confidential settlements to keep hazard evidence out of public view, at a cost to consumers and workers exposed to the same risks.

industries.industry: Sponsors of private judicial seminars (industry-funded legal foundations and law schools)
industries.note: Companies and interest groups that fund luxury educational seminars for judges — the same industries that often have cases in court — would be banned from giving judges travel, lodging, and meals in connection with those events, with a public fund substituting taxpayer-paid attendance.
